WELCOME TO THE PRIMITIVE PITS FAMILY! 
 
 
 
“Because it’s great barbecue we’re after” 
 
Welcome to Primitive Pits 
Thank you for choosing Primitive Pits. We are very proud of our product, 
handcrafted right here in the United States. Please review the information in 
this packet carefully, as it will provide valuable instruction and useful tips 
when using your new Primitive Pits offset smoker. Instructional videos are 
also available on our Primitive Pits YouTube page.  
 
* DANGER, WARNINGS, and CAUTIONS * 
•  Failure to follow the “Dangers, Warnings, and Cautions” may result in 
serious bodily injury, death, or fire. 
• Read this manual completely before using your Primitive Pits Smoker for 
the first time. 
• Do not use indoors! This smoker is for outdoor use only. 
• Do not leave pets, infants, or children unattended near a smoker while in 
use. 
• Keep the grill a minimum of 12 inches away from combustible surfaces. 
• Do not use lighter fluid, gasoline, or any other highly flammable fluids to 
ignite or re-ignite your smoker. 
• Do not use or store lighter fluid, gasoline or any other highly flammable 
fluids within five feet of the smoker. 
• Do not transport your grill while operating or when the grill is hot. Make 
sure the fire is out and the grill is cool before moving. 
• Exterior surfaces on the grill will be hot when in use and during cool down. 
• Should a grease fire occur, keep all doors closed and the top stack baffle 
shut until the fire is out.  This will starve the oxygen and the fire will not 
sustain. 
• Use heat resistant gloves when operating the grill. 
ITEM 23
23 - 32

<!-- page 542 -->
• Do not remove any ash until the fire has completely burned out and is fully 
extinguished. 
• Check www.primitivepits.com for more information on updates and new 
product information. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Getting Started with your New Primitive Pit 
Place your Primitive Pits smoker on a level, fireproof surface at least 12 
inches away from any combustible surface. 
 
LOOSE COMPONENTS FOR YOUR NEW PRIMITIVE PIT CAN BE FOUND 
INSIDE THE FIREBOX.   
 
Thermometers:  
Every Primitive Pit will come with auto calibrated TelTru thermometers, the 
most reliable temp gauge in the industry.  To date, our company has 
shipped over 20,000 TelTru thermometers with no known defects.   
 
We do not recommend using anything to tighten thermometers.  We 
recommend hand tightening to 3 o'clock and then use a wrench (adjustable 
is fine) to finish tightening up 1/4 of a turn. 
 
Care and Maintenance  
We manufacture each smoker from raw steel materials.  At the completion 
of each build, we clean each smoker out preparing for it to be shipped or 
picked up.  In transit to its new home, the smoker will have tiny metal 
fragments and metal residue fall or blow around the smoker.  We advise 
you to pressure wash or hose off the grates before the first cook.  After 
washing or pressure washing the grates, you can air dry and re-apply oil 
(Canola oil, Pam, tallow, etc).  In the sunlight you will be able to further 
inspect the grates. 
ITEM 23
23 - 33

<!-- page 543 -->
Cleaning Cooking Grates 
Wash new grates with warm soapy water and air dry before lightly coating 
with vegetable oil and placing them back in your smoker. After the first 
cook, grates can be cleaned by using a long-handled grill brush. 
 
Seasoning 
Seasoning your new offset prior to your first cook is a vital step in getting 
your offset ready for some low and slow barbecue.   
 
To season, you should liberally coat all grates with a food safe oil in a new, 
clean spray bottle.  
 
In addition, coat the interior of the cooking chamber (only) with a food safe 
oil. Do not add oil to the firebox.  
 
Our choice for oil is canola oil for the grates and inside the chamber.  
There are a multitude of good food grade, high smoke point oils in the 
marketplace.  Olive Oil, Grapeseed Oil, Soy Oil, etc., all can be found at 
your local grocery store. 
 
Once you have sprayed food grade oil on the grates and inside the cooking 
chamber, you can then start a fire and begin to slowly raise the 
temperature.  
 
As with smoking meat, you need to establish a good coal bed.  Our 
objective is to run a clean smoke stack, so more seasoned wood tends to 
work better for the seasoning process.   
 
*During this initial seasoning/burnout, keep the cooking chamber 200-275 
degrees Fahrenheit. DO NOT heat the chamber above 275 degrees 
Fahrenheit and DO NOT attempt to cook any food during this process.  
Burn for a minimum of four (4) hours, but preferably six (6) hours.  After 
four (4) hours, you could add a meat (such as ground beef) to assist in the 
seasoning process.   
 
ITEM 23
23 - 34

<!-- page 544 -->
This initial burn will give you an opportunity to begin to learn the 
responsiveness of the unit as you load splits of wood.  As the unit burns off 
the oil and begins to season the metal you will begin to see clean smoke 
coming out of the stack. 
 
You will see a lot of smoke in the early first hours of the seasoning process.   
This is the oil burning off slowly and beginning to create the needed 
environment for barbecue. 
 
On occasion, grease may find its way through a “worm hole” in the weld.  
This hole is not a leak. This is normal and no cause for concern. As you 
cook and season your smoker, this worm hole will clog.  You can also 
apply food grade silicon to the spot. We also suggest not using excessive 
amounts of oil on the inside of your smoker when seasoning.   
 
Maintaining the exterior of your smoker 
 
Patina/Raw Finish Smokers 
For our raw, patina tank smokers, minimal maintenance is needed.  The 
patina on the tank acts as a protective finish on the smoker.  Linseed oil 
can be used on the exterior of the smoker to protect against rusting/aging, 
and even gives it a bit of a shine. NEVER USE LINSEED OIL ON THE 
INTERIOR OF THE SMOKER. 
 
Custom Painted Smokers 
Painted smokers cannot withstand temperatures over 325 degrees 
Fahrenheit.  (Avoid high temperatures as it is also not recommended for 
cooking.)  High temperatures can and will cause paint to discolor and 
possibly bubble.  Additionally, discoloration is normal on the firebox door 
face due to exposure to fire and soot.  Keep a painted smoker clean by 
hosing it off with water and mild soap.   
 
 
CAUTION: Rags soaked in Linseed Oil can SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUST 
and cause fire.  Place disposed rags in a can or jar full of water and seal. 
Rags not disposed of properly can cause fire damage, serious injury, or 
even death.  
ITEM 23
23 - 35

<!-- page 545 -->
Cleaning 
The more you cook, the more seasoned your smoker will become, but with 
seasoning comes a habitat for bacteria and of course fires. We don’t want 
either of these! 
 
Bacteria will begin to grow if your smoker is not used for long periods of 
time. It is important to clean the grates and the bottom interior floor of the 
unit after each cook.  We recommend a 4” paint scraper.  Stainless steel is 
preferred, but a plastic scraper will suffice.  Scrape the bottom from the 
grate down to the center point of the bottom.  Scoop out and throw away. 
 
Cleaning the grates is also essential after each cook.   You can use a grill 
safe brush but be very careful not to leave any wire remains on the grate 
surface. It is never a fun day to bite down on a tasty piece of barbecue with 
a metal brush bristle stuck to it. We even recommend using a nylon brush 
or again a 4” scraper. 
 
It is always important to get your cooking chamber up to 200 degrees 
Fahrenheit for a minimum of 30-minutes prior to placing meat on the 
grate.  This will also help in providing a food safe environment in your 
smoker.  There are several ways to accomplish this: 1) You can slowly 
acclimate the chamber, taking the heat of the chamber up in an estimated 
hour and fifteen (15) minutes. 2) You can bring the chamber temperature 
slightly higher at 275-285 degrees Fahrenheit, and then let it cool down to 
the desired starting temperature.  This ensures that all of the steel chamber 
is up to temp.  
 
At the beginning of the season and then before storing away for long 
periods of time, de-grease the interior with a citrus based cleaning 
solution. Always make sure your smoker is completely cool before 
disposing of ash or cleaning the chamber. A stiff brushed can be used to 
clean any build-up on the inside of your smoker. If storing for a long period 
of time, you can liberally re-oil the grates and chamber again (once it is 
100% dry). 
 
 
Fire Management Tips 
ITEM 23
23 - 36

<!-- page 546 -->
Always use dry, 20% moisture or less wood. The optimal coal bed is 18” x 
24”. Keep the stack open, and the firebox door cracked. Stack the cook 
wood log-cabin style. If you have a top rack, start out just using/cooking 
on the main grates. Dial in the temp/fire management just using the main 
grates then move on to cooking with the top racks. 
 
Safety Recommendations: 
If you don’t keep your smoker clean, there is a chance the fire from the 
firebox will jump into chamber.  Always keep a clean smoker! 
 
Never store the smoker indoors while cooking and always let the smoker 
cool 24 hours before moving back into a shed, garage or indoors.    
 
Make sure the firebox is empty and no ash remains in the firebox before 
moving the smoker indoors.   Ash can stay hot for 24-48 hours after you’ve 
placed your last split in the firebox. 
 
In the case of a fire inside your cooking chamber, the easiest and safest 
way to stop the fire is to 1. Shut the firebox door and firebox baffle, 2. Shut 
the smokestack and keep the chamber door closed. It’s better to lose 
barbecue than to have an out of control fire.  Closing down the smoker will 
stop the fire.  Without oxygen, fire cannot survive. 
   
* IMPORTANT SAFTEY NOTICE! 
 
Rags soaked in Linseed Oil can SPONTANEOUSLY COMBUST and cause 
fire.  Place disposed rags in a can or jar full of water and seal. Rags not 
disposed of properly can cause fire damage, serious injury, or even death.

RE:

Office of Coastal and Ocean Management  
We are seeking your approval to send a letter requesting a presentation from the Maryland Department of Natural 
Resources’ (DNR) Office of Coastal and Ocean Management at an upcoming meeting. 
DNR has been tasked with developing an offshore wind – fisheries compensation plan. The department is becoming 
increasingly aware of the impact of US Wind’s proposed operation and maintenance facility on the commercial 
fishing industry. To date, they’ve met with the commercial fisherman at least twice and are interested in a discussion 
with the county.

RE: 
Board Room Use Request for Snow Hill Town Meetings 
We have received a request from the Town of Snow Hill to utilize the board room, adjacent to the commissioner 
chambers, for their town meetings. 
The Mayor and Council meet monthly on the second Tuesday of each month at 7pm. They also routinely meeting 
on the first and last Tuesday of each month for a work session, starting at 5pm. Other board and commission 
meetings of the Town would take place elsewhere.  
Other considerations to be worked out include staffing of the security vestibule, any potential schedule conflicts, 
and if the Town would like to piggyback on our contract with Swagit for recording and editing of the meetings. 
We seek your approval to pursue this arrangement, utilizing this county space and its audio and visual technology, 
in a fashion that is cost-neutral to the county.
